title: Space exploration
subtitle: From early rockets to Voyager, SpaceX and the Dutch contribution, through films, series and documentaries.
introNote: Thirteen choices: four dramatic films, one dramatic miniseries and eight documentary films, series or episodes. The expanded route adds SpaceX’s development and Inspiration4, Voyager’s later ground team, and Dutch perspectives through Wubbo Ockels and André Kuipers. First Man and Apollo 13 remain optional close-ups alongside From the Earth to the Moon; The Farthest and It’s Quieter in the Twilight offer complementary Voyager eras. Watching everything is about 37 hours 45 minutes, using an hour per Apollo-series episode and the editions described in the title notes. IMDb scores were checked on 30 October 2026 through publicly indexed pages; a dash marks an unverified score, not zero. Scores measure reception, not reliability. Documentary bars describe the historical subject or observed operations; interviews and brief archive do not extend them. A long envelope can contain jumps, and c. marks approximate boundaries.
scopeNote: This is a selective route, not a complete history or a ranking. Dutch space activity appears through astronomy satellites, ESTEC, CubeSats, atmospheric instruments and astronauts: these are distinct national and international contributions, rather than a single independent Dutch launch program. ESTEC is an ESA center in the Netherlands; TROPOMI is a Dutch instrument on a European satellite. The viewing choices still lean American and European. Japanese exploration, the full Soviet/Russian and Chinese programs, space law, commercial constellations and many failed missions need a broader guide. Unconnected stops mark gaps in the screen selection. SpaceX films have close participant access and are read alongside mission and regulatory sources. Space fantasy and alternate-history series, including the 2019 For All Mankind, remain outside this historical selection.
closingNote: The expanded historical spine ends with completed SpaceX milestones in 2024, including Polaris Dawn and the first Super Heavy tower catch. These later stops are context beyond the selected SpaceX films’ story years, not claims that those films depict them. This is not a live mission tracker or a claim that exploration stopped in 2024. Agency, university, museum, broadcaster and regulatory records provide the historical checks; no streaming availability or subtitle support is guaranteed.

events.title: A rocket runs on liquid fuel
events.description: Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket in Massachusetts. The short flight demonstrated a propulsion approach that would help make spaceflight possible; it did not reach space.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: The rocket’s violent inheritance
events.description: Nazi Germany deployed V-2 ballistic missiles against cities. Their production depended on concentration-camp prisoners and lethal forced labor. The technology’s later place in spaceflight cannot erase the people killed making and using it.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Before orbit, the sound barrier
events.description: Chuck Yeager’s X-1 flight belongs to experimental aviation. The Right Stuff uses this world of test pilots to introduce the skills, risks and mythology that surrounded the first American astronauts.

sources.label: AFI · The Right Stuff story and production record

events.title: Sputnik makes orbit real
events.description: The Soviet Union launched the first artificial Earth satellite. A scientific achievement became a Cold War shock, accelerating the competition that shaped the early space programs.

sources.label: NASA · Dawn of the Space Age

events.title: The Moon becomes a destination
events.description: Soviet Luna 2 reached the lunar surface by impact; Luna 3 returned the first views of the far side. These robotic achievements preceded the human Moon landings by a decade.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: People reach space
events.description: Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space and in orbit aboard Vostok 1. Alan Shepard followed with the first American spaceflight, a suborbital mission. Orbit and a brief flight into space are different achievements.

events.title: The mathematics behind an orbit
events.description: John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth. Hidden Figures shifts the viewpoint to Katherine Johnson and her colleagues at Langley, whose calculations and engineering work helped make the missions possible.

sources.label: NASA · The women behind Hidden Figures

events.title: A spacecraft visits another planet
events.description: Mariner 2 flew past Venus, completing the first successful planetary encounter. Exploration was already branching beyond the race to put people on the Moon.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: The first woman in space
events.description: Valentina Tereshkova launched aboard Vostok 6. This Soviet milestone is absent from the American-centered dramas in the viewing route; the shared year with Mercury’s final flight does not imply a screen connection.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Learning to work outside a capsule
events.description: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk. The American Gemini program developed the endurance, rendezvous and maneuvering experience needed for Apollo. First Man depicts Armstrong’s Gemini training and later mission rather than Leonov’s flight.

events.title: A soft landing before Apollo
events.description: Luna 9 made the first successful soft landing on the Moon and transmitted pictures from the surface. Soviet robotic exploration remained an important part of lunar history.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: A fire on the launch pad
events.description: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee died during an Apollo ground test. The disaster exposed lethal weaknesses in the spacecraft and test environment before Apollo’s crewed flights began.

events.title: A European space center in the Dutch dunes
events.description: After its early years in Delft, ESTEC opened its Noordwijk site. This is ESA’s European technical center, hosted by the Netherlands, rather than a separate Dutch launch agency. Dutch space activity combines national research and industry with European and international missions.

sources.label: ESA · ESTEC opens in Noordwijk in 1968

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: People orbit the Moon
events.description: Apollo 8 carried Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders around the Moon. It was a lunar-orbit mission, not a landing, and a crucial step beyond Earth orbit.

events.title: The first lunar landing
events.description: Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon while Michael Collins remained in orbit. First Man follows Armstrong; From the Earth to the Moon offers a wider view of the program and the people behind it.

events.title: Getting home becomes the mission
events.description: An oxygen-tank accident forced Apollo 13 to abandon its landing. The crew used the lunar module as a refuge while teams on Earth worked through the problems of power, air and a safe return.

events.title: Spaceflight becomes a place to stay
events.description: The Soviet Union launched Salyut 1, the first space station. Long stays in orbit opened a different line of exploration from short expeditions to the Moon.

sources.label: ESA · Major achievements in human spaceflight

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Apollo ends with field science
events.description: Apollo 17 completed the program’s final lunar landing. The later missions emphasized longer surface stays and geology; From the Earth to the Moon follows the work beyond the famous first landing.

events.title: The Netherlands puts astronomy into orbit
events.description: The Astronomische Nederlandse Satelliet, ANS, carried Dutch and American ultraviolet and X-ray instruments into Earth orbit. Dutch laboratories and industry could build a scientific satellite while relying on an international launch service.

sources.label: SRON · ANS mission and Dutch instruments

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Rivals meet in orbit
events.description: American Apollo and Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked, and their crews met in space. Compatible systems and joint operations offered a different model from the earlier race.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: A laboratory on Mars
events.description: Viking 1 landed on Mars and returned surface images and experiments. Its search for evidence of life illustrates the difference between collecting measurements and having a simple answer to a scientific question.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Two probes head for the giant planets
events.description: Voyager 2 launched before Voyager 1. Their trajectories used planetary gravity assists to explore the outer planets; the Golden Records carried a small selection of Earth’s sounds, images and greetings.

events.title: Two encounters transform Jupiter
events.description: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 passed Jupiter on 5 March and 9 July. Images revealed active volcanism on Io and intricate structures in the planet’s atmosphere and rings. The Farthest makes the encounter teams and scientific surprises part of its planetary tour.

events.title: Saturn divides the routes
events.description: Voyager 1 encountered Saturn and Titan in November 1980; its Titan trajectory took it away from the path to Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 visited Saturn in August 1981 and continued toward those outer planets. The spacecraft followed different tours, not identical journeys.

events.title: The Shuttle takes flight
events.description: Columbia launched on STS-1, the Space Shuttle’s first flight. A reusable orbiter promised a new way of working in Earth orbit, but the system remained technically demanding and dangerous.

events.title: Dutch space science joins an infrared sky survey
events.description: IRAS was a joint Netherlands–United States–United Kingdom mission. Its cooled telescope surveyed the infrared sky, uncovering sources hidden from visible-light observations. It illustrates a Dutch contribution that reached far beyond human spaceflight.

sources.label: JPL · IRAS and its international partners

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Wubbo Ockels flies aboard Spacelab D1
events.description: ESA astronaut Wubbo Ockels became the first Dutch citizen in space on Challenger’s STS-61A mission, conducting research in the German Spacelab D1 laboratory. Dutch-born Lodewijk van den Berg had flown earlier in 1985 as an American astronaut; birthplace and citizenship are different distinctions.

sources.label: ESA · Dutch-born astronaut Lodewijk van den Berg

events.title: The only close encounter with Uranus
events.description: Voyager 2 passed Uranus, studying its atmosphere, rings, moons and unusual magnetic environment. Its 1989 Neptune encounter was still ahead. This stop belongs to Voyager’s robotic tour, a separate story from the Challenger disaster four days later.

events.title: A launch decision becomes a disaster
events.description: Challenger broke apart during ascent, killing all seven crew members. The documentary series examines the booster-joint concerns and organizational decisions as well as the lives lost.

events.title: Voyager reaches Neptune
events.description: Voyager 2 flew past Neptune after visiting Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus. The Farthest follows how small teams turned fleeting encounters into discoveries about planets, rings and moons.

events.title: Voyager looks back at Earth
events.description: Voyager 1 photographed Earth as a tiny point of light in a wider Solar System portrait. The Pale Blue Dot is an image from the mission, not a photograph taken after the 2012 heliopause crossing.

events.title: A telescope that can be repaired
events.description: Hubble launched into Earth orbit with a flaw in its primary mirror. The 1993 servicing mission installed corrective equipment. Space exploration also means observing the universe, not only traveling toward other worlds.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: An international station takes shape
events.description: Zarya and Unity, the first two International Space Station elements, launched and were joined in orbit. The project brought together hardware and work from multiple countries on an unprecedented scale.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Another Shuttle crew is lost
events.description: Columbia broke apart during re-entry, killing all seven people aboard. This is a separate accident seventeen years after Challenger, beyond the documentary series’ main story.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Two robotic geologists arrive
events.description: Spirit and Opportunity landed on Mars after their 2003 launches. Their investigations of rocks and soils helped reconstruct the planet’s watery past. Good Night Oppy follows the rovers and the people operating them across years of changing conditions.

events.title: André Kuipers takes Dutch experiments to the ISS
events.description: Kuipers made his first spaceflight on the Dutch-government-sponsored DELTA mission, traveling in a Russian Soyuz spacecraft and working aboard the International Space Station. Dutch participation operated through ESA and international transport and facilities.

sources.label: ESA Archives · Kuipers and the DELTA experiments

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: A landing on Titan
events.description: ESA’s Huygens probe descended through Titan’s atmosphere and transmitted from the surface. Delivered by the joint NASA–ESA–ASI Cassini-Huygens mission, it extended surface exploration to a moon of Saturn.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: A university builds a working satellite
events.description: TU Delft’s Delfi-C3 launched from India. The student-built CubeSat tested technology and trained engineers, showing how a national space sector also grows through universities, small spacecraft and industrial partnerships.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Falcon 1 reaches orbit
events.description: SpaceX’s fourth Falcon 1 flight reached orbit after three failures. Return to Space uses the company’s early launch struggle as background to its later NASA crew mission. Reaching orbit came before recovering and reusing Falcon 9 boosters.

sources.label: Netflix · From Falcon 1 to Crew Dragon

events.title: Kuipers lives and works in orbit
events.description: Kuipers returned aboard Soyuz for ESA’s PromISSe mission, serving on ISS Expeditions 30 and 31. Cosmic Encounters includes his onboard footage and scientific work; Alexander Gerst’s training is another strand, not a claim that Gerst flew with Kuipers.

sources.label: ZDF Studios · Cosmic Encounters and 50-minute edition

events.title: Commercial cargo reaches the station
events.description: Dragon became the first commercial spacecraft to be attached to the ISS. This was an uncrewed demonstration under NASA’s COTS program, distinct from the 2020 crew flight. Kuipers was aboard the station during the visit; that overlap alone does not establish a scene in Cosmic Encounters.

sources.label: Netflix · From Falcon 1 to Crew Dragon

events.title: Beyond the solar wind’s bubble
events.description: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause into interstellar space. It left the heliosphere, not the entire gravitational domain of the Sun: “leaving the solar system” is an imprecise shortcut for this boundary.

events.title: India reaches Mars
events.description: ISRO’s Mars Orbiter Mission, also called Mangalyaan, entered orbit around Mars on India’s first attempt. It made interplanetary navigation and science part of a widening international story.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: A comet gets a visitor
events.description: ESA’s Rosetta mission delivered the Philae lander to comet 67P. The orbiter’s longer investigation mattered as well as the landing: a comet could now be studied up close as it changed near the Sun.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Pluto comes into focus
events.description: New Horizons made the first close flyby of Pluto, revealing a complex world in the Kuiper Belt. Robotic encounters continued to change the map long after Voyager’s planetary tour.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: An orbital-launch booster comes back
events.description: After delivering satellites toward orbit, a Falcon 9 first stage returned for a controlled landing at Cape Canaveral. The recovered stage had supported an orbital launch; the booster itself did not complete an orbit. The upper stage was not recovered.

events.title: A recovered booster flies again
events.description: The SES-10 launch reused a Falcon 9 first stage. Landing and reflight are different milestones: reusable launch systems require inspection, refurbishment and another successful flight, rather than recovery alone.

events.title: Dutch technology measures the atmosphere
events.description: The Dutch-built TROPOMI instrument launched aboard the European Sentinel-5P satellite to map atmospheric gases and air pollution. KNMI, SRON, TNO and Airbus DS-NL contributed. This is a Dutch instrument on an international spacecraft, not an entirely Dutch satellite.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Falcon Heavy makes its first flight
events.description: SpaceX demonstrated a launch vehicle built around three Falcon-derived cores. The two side boosters returned to landing zones. This added lift capability alongside the separate development of Dragon crew transport and, later, Starship.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Voyager 2 crosses the heliopause
events.description: Voyager 2 joined Voyager 1 in interstellar space six years later. Its working plasma instrument provided a different set of direct measurements at the boundary. The Farthest predates this crossing; It’s Quieter in the Twilight picks up the later operational era.

sources.label: NASA · Comparing the two heliopause crossings

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: The first landing on the lunar far side
events.description: China’s Chang’e-4 made the first soft landing on the Moon’s far side, using the Queqiao relay satellite for communications. The far side is not permanently dark; it is the hemisphere facing away from Earth.

sources.label: CNSA · Chang’e-4 lands on the lunar far side

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Opportunity’s mission is declared complete
events.description: Opportunity last communicated in June 2018 during a planet-wide dust storm. NASA declared the mission complete in February 2019 after attempts to regain contact. The final year on this documentary’s span includes that recovery effort.

events.title: A commercial spacecraft carries NASA crew
events.description: Demo-2 launched Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley aboard SpaceX’s Crew Dragon toward the International Space Station. It tested a commercially provided crew transport system within NASA’s program.

events.title: Exploration depends on the ground team
events.description: Upgrades to Canberra’s DSS43 antenna temporarily prevented commands from being sent to Voyager 2. A test command on 29 October received a reply. It’s Quieter in the Twilight follows the people and aging systems behind this continuing work, rather than repeating only the planetary flybys.

sources.label: NASA · Voyager 2 and the upgraded Canberra dish
Filmmaker · It’s Quieter in the Twilight
Billy Miossi · Filming began in June 2019

events.title: A privately funded crew orbits Earth
events.description: Inspiration4 carried Jared Isaacman, Sian Proctor, Hayley Arceneaux and Chris Sembroski aboard Crew Dragon on a three-day orbital flight. It did not visit the ISS. Countdown follows their selection, training, launch and return; its charity-centered presentation is part of the mission’s own public story.

events.title: A new view of the universe
events.description: The NASA–ESA–CSA James Webb Space Telescope released its first science images and spectra after launching in December 2021. Infrared observations extended the reach of space astronomy.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: An uncrewed test around the Moon
events.description: Artemis I tested the Space Launch System and Orion on an uncrewed lunar flight and return. A successful test is a milestone in its own right; this stop makes no prediction about later missions.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: Starship and Super Heavy begin integrated flight tests
events.description: The first integrated Starship–Super Heavy launch ended in vehicle loss. It was a development test, not a completed orbital mission or a crew flight. The FAA’s mishap investigation required corrective actions before further launches.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: India lands in the southern lunar highlands
events.description: Chandrayaan-3 landed at about 69° south latitude, bringing the Vikram lander and Pragyan rover to the Moon. It was a landing in the southern high latitudes, not at the geographic south pole.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: A commercial spacewalk from Dragon
events.description: Polaris Dawn tested SpaceX’s new EVA suits during the first commercial spacewalk. Jared Isaacman and Sarah Gillis exited in turn while all four crew members experienced the depressurized cabin. This was a later mission, outside Countdown’s 2021 story.
events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

events.title: A launch tower catches Super Heavy
events.description: On Starship’s fifth flight test, the Super Heavy booster returned to the launch site and was caught by the tower arms. It demonstrated one element of the proposed reusable system, not recovery of both stages or completion of a crew-rated vehicle.

sources.label: NASA Inspector General · Starship test history and Flight 5 catch

events.gapNote: Historical context · no selected title directly covers this milestone.

entries.title: The Right Stuff
entries.premise: From Chuck Yeager’s experimental flights to the Mercury Seven, pilots and families face a new kind of risk and celebrity.
entries.learn: How test flying, politics and public image shaped Project Mercury. Treat the characterization of Gus Grissom with care: the film’s suggestion of panic is not an established explanation of his capsule’s hatch accident.
entries.coverageNote: The 1947 X-1 sequence is a substantial opening chapter. AFI’s synopsis then moves to Edwards in 1952 and follows Mercury to Gordon Cooper’s 1963 flight, so 1948–1951 stay empty. Use the 1983 Philip Kaufman film, not the 2020 TV adaptation. The film also exaggerates the danger to Glenn’s mission; it is a drama rather than a literal mission record.

sources.label: Smithsonian · Mercury and First Man’s dramatic liberties

entries.title: Hidden Figures
entries.premise: Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson work through technical problems and racial and gender barriers at Langley.
entries.learn: The mathematics, computing and often overlooked people behind early American spaceflight. The film compresses careers and invents or combines characters and confrontations; its chronology should not replace the women’s biographies.
entries.coverageNote: The central film narrative concentrates on 1961–1962 and Glenn’s orbit. A childhood prologue is excluded. Vaughan became a supervisor in 1949 and Jackson an engineer in 1958, earlier than the film’s compressed story suggests. Those real dates do not extend the film’s story bars.

sources.label: NASA · Hidden Figures and the 1962 mission

entries.title: First Man
entries.premise: Neil Armstrong’s professional life and family grief unfold across the testing, training and missions leading to Apollo 11.
entries.learn: Why reaching the Moon took years of incremental flight experience, engineering and personal sacrifice. Its intimate reading of Armstrong’s grief is a dramatic interpretation, including the unverified bracelet scene on the Moon.
entries.coverageNote: The Smithsonian identifies the film’s span as 1961–1969. Armstrong’s Gemini 8 flight in 1966 falls within that continuous career narrative. The 1965 event connection introduces the broader Gemini program; it does not claim Armstrong made Leonov’s first spacewalk.

sources.label: Smithsonian · What First Man got right

entries.title: From the Earth to the Moon
entries.premise: Twelve dramatic chapters follow Apollo through astronauts, engineers, controllers, geologists and families.
entries.learn: The program beyond a single heroic flight: design choices, failure investigations, training and lunar science. Watch the complete series for breadth; it overlaps First Man and Apollo 13, which offer more concentrated alternatives.
entries.coverageNote: The main historical story runs from 1961 to the last Apollo landing in 1972. The final episode’s scenes about Georges Méliès and his 1902 film are a parallel artistic frame, not an extension of Apollo’s coverage. All 12 episodes are included, budgeted at about 60 minutes each; editions vary. It remains scripted drama, with reconstructed dialogue and composite storytelling.

entries.title: Apollo 13
entries.premise: A routine lunar expedition becomes an emergency, with three astronauts and teams on Earth trying to bring a damaged spacecraft home.
entries.learn: The practical work of mission control, limited resources and engineering under pressure. The broad rescue is historical, while dialogue and interpersonal tension are shaped for the film.
entries.coverageNote: The central story is the 1970 preparation, flight and return. The opening remembrance of Apollo 1 and the Apollo 11 television celebration establish background and do not create earlier coverage bars. Use Ron Howard’s 1995 feature; the budget is 140 minutes. This is an optional close-up of ground also covered differently in the miniseries.

entries.title: The Farthest
entries.premise: Voyager’s scientists and engineers recall sending two small spacecraft past giant planets and toward interstellar space.
entries.learn: Gravity assists, long-lived engineering and the scientific surprises of robotic exploration. Archive material and retrospective interviews tell the mission; interviews filmed decades later do not extend the historical span. The encounters are now separated on the timeline so Voyager 1’s route through Titan is not confused with Voyager 2’s onward flight to Uranus and Neptune.
entries.coverageNote: The PBS transcript explicitly dates mission preparation to 1972 and follows the 1977 launches, planetary encounters through 1989 and Voyager 1’s 2012 heliopause crossing. This is a mission-history envelope, not a claim that every intervening year receives a scene. Budget the 121-minute feature; the linked PBS presentation is a shorter 97-minute broadcast cut. “Left the solar system” in publicity means the heliosphere here, not the Sun’s full gravitational domain. This 2017 film cannot cover Voyager 2’s 2018 heliopause crossing or later operations; those have separate context stops and a later documentary.

sources.label: PBS · Film and transcript, including 1972 preparation

entries.title: Wubbo: een Hollander in de ruimte

eventNotes.ockels: Selection, training and the D1 flight

entries.premise: An Andere Tijden episode follows Ockels from a Dutch recruitment advertisement through years of training and setbacks to Spacelab D1.
entries.learn: How a Dutch scientist reached space through ESA and NASA, and how national enthusiasm related to a European research mission. Dutch-language interviews and archive give this route a local perspective.
entries.coverageNote: The broadcaster’s account dates the recruitment advertisement to 1977, followed by European selection in 1978 and the 1985 flight. Its brief introduction anticipating Kuipers’s 2011 launch is excluded. The page gives 30 minutes and December 2011 publication/broadcast information. A matching IMDb episode identity and score were not verified, so the dash means unverified rather than zero. The broadcaster and museum catalogue contain inconsistent shorthand dates; ESA’s 30 October 1985 launch date is used for the historical stop.

sources.label: Andere Tijden · Wubbo: een Hollander in de ruimte

entries.title: Challenger: The Final Flight
entries.premise: Engineers, officials and relatives reconstruct the Challenger disaster and the decisions that preceded it.
entries.learn: How technical warnings, launch expectations and institutional judgment can interact. The four-part documentary centers people and decisions; it does not cover the entire Shuttle era or the later Columbia accident.
entries.coverageNote: The main historical arc begins with the new astronaut generation selected in 1978 and builds through the 1986 loss and investigation. Earlier program archive and later remembrance are context rather than extra story bars. The start is an editorial boundary, not an exact date for every archival image. All four episodes are included: Netflix lists 44, 41, 41 and 52 minutes, totaling 178 minutes.

entries.title: Good Night Oppy

eventNotes.oppy-farewell: Last contact and end of mission

entries.premise: The teams behind Spirit and Opportunity build, land and care for robotic explorers that outlast their planned missions.
entries.learn: How rover operations become field geology at a distance, and how discoveries accumulate over years. The surface journeys include visual-effects reconstructions; these are not continuous camera footage shot by an observer on Mars.
entries.coverageNote: The span includes the rover project’s development from around 2000, the 2003 launches, 2004 landings and the recovery attempts ending in 2019. The development boundary is approximate. Opportunity’s last signal was in June 2018; the mission declaration came in February 2019. The film’s present-day interviews are excluded from the bar. The early planning material is not intended as a year-by-year history.

entries.title: Return to Space
entries.premise: NASA astronauts, their families and SpaceX teams prepare for Demo-2 while the film retraces the company’s earlier rocket development.
entries.learn: The progression from Falcon 1 to Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon, alongside NASA’s role in buying and supporting commercial transport. The filmmakers have close access to the company; this is a participant-centered account, not a comprehensive audit of private spaceflight.
entries.coverageNote: The historical envelope begins around SpaceX’s 2002 founding and culminates in the 2020 Demo-2 mission and splashdown. Netflix describes a nearly twenty-year journey and explicitly identifies Falcon 1, reusable Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon. The early boundary is approximate and the film jumps over years. Earlier Apollo/Shuttle archive supplies background. It does not cover the 2021 Inspiration4 flight or Starship’s later integrated tests.

sources.label: Netflix · Return to Space production notes
Netflix · From Falcon 1 to Crew Dragon

entries.title: Cosmic Encounters
entries.premise: André Kuipers films life aboard the ISS while Alexander Gerst trains on Earth for a future mission.
entries.learn: Dutch participation within European human spaceflight: research, daily life, training and cooperation at the station. This was made for ZDF and ARTE, with a Dutch astronaut as one guide; it is not a survey of the entire Dutch space sector.
entries.coverageNote: The central onboard footage belongs to Kuipers’s 2011–2012 PromISSe mission. Gerst’s training anticipates his 2014 flight; the flight itself is not depicted and does not extend the bar to 2014. The 2011 start of the combined preparation/mission envelope is approximate. ZDF’s international catalogue lists a 50-minute edition, used here; IMDb and some home-video listings give 55 minutes. Also circulated as Encounter in Space / Rencontre dans l’espace. The 2012 production is distinct from later distribution and classification dates.

sources.label: ZDF Studios · Cosmic Encounters and 50-minute edition

entries.title: It's Quieter in the Twilight
entries.premise: A small Voyager flight team keeps the probes working as hardware ages, expertise becomes harder to replace and the pandemic interrupts ordinary routines.
entries.learn: What exploration looks like decades after launch: patient troubleshooting, ground infrastructure and the people who hold a mission’s knowledge. Pair it with The Farthest for the difference between spectacular flybys and long-term operations.
entries.coverageNote: Director Billy Miossi says filming began in June 2019 and continued for about eighteen months. The approximate 2019–2020 bar follows that observed operational period; old launch footage and the engineers’ career memories do not turn it into a continuous 1977–2022 history. The 2018 Voyager 2 crossing is background. The film premiered at SXSW in 2022; many platforms label its wider release 2023. Apple’s listing rounds the running time to 84 minutes; other listings give 83. Later Voyager repairs are not presumed to appear in this film.

sources.label: Filmmaker · It’s Quieter in the Twilight
Billy Miossi · Filming began in June 2019

entries.title: Countdown: Inspiration4 Mission to Space

eventNotes.inspiration4: Selection, training, orbital flight and return

entries.premise: Five episodes follow four privately funded crew members from selection through training to a three-day journey aboard Crew Dragon.
entries.learn: How a private orbital mission is organized and how its crew prepares. The charity and inspiration narrative comes from close access to the participants; the series does not establish that private orbital flight is broadly affordable or accessible.
entries.coverageNote: The central mission and preparation take place in 2021. Childhood stories and personal biographies are framing material, not extra mission years. All five episodes are included. Netflix lists 47, 46, 48, 39 and 68 minutes, totaling 248 minutes; episode five includes launch, flight and return. Florida’s 15–18 September dates correspond to a launch after midnight UTC on 16 September. This is Inspiration4, not the later Polaris Dawn mission.

sources.label: Netflix · Final episode covers flight and return
